sigma:
title: LockBit 3.0 BYOVD Driver Loading
status: experimental
logsource:
  category: driver_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\RTCore64.sys'
      - '\DBUtil_2_3.sys'
  condition: selection
yara:
rule LockBit3_Encryptor {
  meta:
    description = "Detects LockBit 3.0 ransomware encryptor"
    author = "Threat-Intel-Toolkit"
    date = "2026-03-29"
  strings:
    $s1 = ".restoretext" wide
    $s2 = "LockBit 3.0" ascii wide
  condition:
    uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and all of them
}
kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost_update.exe" or ProcessCommandLine contains "RTCore64.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

hunting_queries.objective: Detect LockBit 3.0 BYOVD driver load via vulnerable RTCore64.sys
hunting_queries.query:
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("RTCore64.sys", "DBUtil_2_3.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
hunting_queries.schema_dependency: DeviceImageLoadEvents (Defender XDR). If only Sysmon is onboarded, map to SecurityEvent/Event with EventID 7 and ImageLoaded.
hunting_queries.tuning: Allowlist signed legitimate RTCore64.sys deployments by SHA256; alert only on unsigned or unexpected FolderPath.
hunting_queries.validation: Load the vulnerable driver in an isolated VM and confirm the rule fires before production.

hunting_queries.objective: Locate the index/sourcetype carrying driver-load telemetry before writing the production detection
hunting_queries.query:
| tstats count where index=* by index, sourcetype
| search sourcetype=*sysmon* OR sourcetype=*WinEventLog*
hunting_queries.schema_dependency: Unknown which index receives Sysmon EID 7 / driver loads. Resolve before authoring the production SPL.
hunting_queries.validation: Confirm the chosen sourcetype emits ImageLoaded with file hashes via: | tstats values(ImageLoaded) where index=CHOSEN_INDEX

examples.name: Family Online Safety Guide
examples.description: Simple guidance for parent protecting family online

input.natural_language_query: How do I protect my kids from online scams and keep our family devices safe?

alert_level.message: No specific threats targeting your profile, but good security habits are always important

friendly_summary.headline: Keeping Your Family Safe Online: A Simple Guide
friendly_summary.message: Great question! Online safety for families doesn't have to be complicated. Here are the most important things you can do, explained simply.

for_the_whole_family.what_it_means: A secret word or phrase that only your family knows. If someone online claims to be a relative or friend asking for help, they should know this password.
for_the_whole_family.why_it_matters: Scammers sometimes pretend to be family members in trouble. This simple trick stops them.
for_the_whole_family.action: Pick a password at your next family dinner and make sure everyone remembers it

for_the_whole_family.tip: Talk about what's okay to share online
for_the_whole_family.what_it_means: Agree as a family on what information is private (address, school name, vacation plans, etc.)
for_the_whole_family.why_it_matters: Information shared online can be used by bad people to target your family
for_the_whole_family.action: Have a 10-minute family conversation about online sharing

for_parents.tip: Set up parental controls on devices
for_parents.what_it_means: Built-in tools that let you control what your kids can access
for_parents.why_it_matters: Protects kids from inappropriate content and limits screen time

how_to.iphone_ipad: Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions

for_parents.what_it_means: Fake emails or messages trying to steal information
red_flags: 😱 Creates panic ('Your account will be deleted!')
🎁 Too good to be true ('You won a prize!')
🔗 Asks you to click a link urgently
✍️ Has spelling mistakes or looks unprofessional
📧 Sender email doesn't match the company
for_parents.what_to_do: When in doubt, don't click. Go directly to the website by typing it yourself.

for_kids_teens.tip: If something feels wrong, tell a parent
for_kids_teens.explanation: Trust your instincts! If someone online makes you uncomfortable, it's always okay to tell mom or dad. You won't get in trouble.
examples: Someone asking you to keep secrets from parents

for_kids_teens.tip: Not everyone online is who they say they are
for_kids_teens.explanation: People can pretend to be anyone online - even other kids. Be careful about who you trust.
for_kids_teens.rule: Never meet someone in person that you only know from online without a parent

device_security_basics.why: Updates fix security problems. Let them install automatically.

device_security_basics.action: Use a PIN or fingerprint to unlock
device_security_basics.why: Stops others from accessing your device if lost
Default passwords are easy for hackers to guess
device_security_basics.difficulty: Medium - check router manual or call your internet provider

scam_alerts_for_families.how_it_works: Someone asks you to buy gift cards and share the codes
scam_alerts_for_families.remember: No legitimate company or government agency asks for gift cards as payment. Ever.
scam_alerts_for_families.if_this_happens: Hang up. It's always a scam.

scam_alerts_for_families.how_it_works: Fun quizzes that ask questions like 'What's your pet's name?' or 'What street did you grow up on?'
scam_alerts_for_families.the_trick: These are often the same questions used for password recovery
scam_alerts_for_families.advice: Skip these quizzes or give fake answers

if_something_goes_wrong: If a child is in danger: contact local police or call 911

examples.name: Attack Path Analysis - Cloud Environment
examples.description: Red team requesting attack chain analysis for AWS environment

input.natural_language_query: What are the most effective attack chains for compromising AWS environments based on recent campaigns?

executive_summary.headline: AWS Attack Chains: Initial Access to Data Exfiltration
key_points: SSRF to IMDS remains most common initial access (40% of cloud breaches)
Exposed credentials in code repositories highly effective
Lambda function abuse for persistence gaining popularity
S3 bucket misconfigurations still prevalent despite awareness

cwe_chains.name: SSRF to cloud credential exposure

links.evidence: SSRF reaching IMDS endpoint in web tier
Over-permissive instance role reused for API access

enabling_conditions: instance role broader than workload needs

break_points.control: Enforce IMDSv2 (token-bound) and egress filtering from the web tier
break_points.rationale: Neutralizes the primary link; the credential-exposure tail cannot start

break_points.control: Scope instance roles to least privilege
break_points.rationale: Caps blast radius if the primary link is ever reached

chain.notes: Works on EC2, ECS, EKS. IMDSv2 requires token but often not enforced.

chain.method: Create Lambda function triggered by CloudWatch event
chain.evasion: Use existing role, blend with legitimate functions

chain.method: aws s3 sync to attacker-controlled bucket
chain.evasion: Use VPC endpoint to avoid CloudTrail data events

tool_recommendations.use_case: Post-compromise enumeration and finding additional attack paths

evasion_techniques.details: Many read-only actions not logged by default in CloudTrail
If SCPs allow access from corporate IPs, pivot through compromised internal host
Temporary credentials harder to track than long-term access keys

detection_opportunities.note: Understanding blue team detection helps improve red team ops
indicators: API calls from unusual geographic locations
Credential usage outside normal business hours
S3 bucket access from new IAM principal
